"If we take these ideas to their logical conclusion, there’s a political agenda to be inferred: we should be actively promoting inclusive digital developments, that is, those that include people who have previously been excluded. We should be breaking down existing inequalities and shaping digital spaces in such a way that participation and fairness are built in from the very beginning. At the same time, this agenda has to consider our ecological responsibilities. We all know that AI systems consume vast amounts of energy.

So digital sovereignty also implies that we need to be aware of the resources we intend to use, so that the technology can be made sustainable. Perhaps we can be more specific about that. Digital sovereignty is therefore not a category for understanding existing power structures and dependencies.

It’s an ethical principle that ought to serve as a moral com pass for development; it’s a normative, positive, optimistic concept for giving the future some orientation and meaning."

Wenn wir diese Ideen konsequent zu Ende denken, lässt sich daraus eine politische Agenda ableiten: Wir sollten aktiv inklusive digitale Entwicklungen fördern, d. h. solche,
die Menschen einbeziehen, die bisher ausgeschlossen waren. Wir sollten bestehende Ungleichheiten abbauen und digitale Räume so gestalten, dass Teilhabe und Fairness von Anfang an fest verankert sind. Gleichzeitig muss diese Agenda unsere ökologischen Verantwortlichkeiten berücksichtigen. Wir alle wissen, dass KI-Systeme enorme Mengen an Energie verbrauchen.

Digitale Souveränität bedeutet also auch, dass wir uns bewusst sein müssen, welche Ressourcen wir nutzen wollen, damit die Technologie nachhaltig gestaltet werden kann. Sie ist ein ethisches Prinzip, das als moralischer Kompass für die Entwicklung dienen soll; sie ist ein normatives, positives, optimistisches Konzept, um der Zukunft Orientierung und Sinn zu geben.

Business leaders don’t need to replace every non‑European tool overnight. Digital sovereignty has become a central political and economic objective for Germany and the European Union. The concept describes the ability of states, companies, institutions, and individuals to act independently, securely, and autonomously in the digital sphere while maintaining control over data, digital infrastructures, and software systems. At the same time, digital sovereignty does not mean complete technological isolation or autarky. Instead, it emphasizes the freedom to choose digital technologies independently and to avoid irreversible dependencies on individual providers.
The debate has intensified due to geopolitical tensions, technological competition, and Europe’s dependence on foreign technology companies, particularly from the United States and China. What began as a mainly regulatory discussion has evolved into a broader question of industrial policy, economic resilience, and geopolitical strategy.

A key takeaway from this article is that the impact of AI in healthcare depends less on capability — and more on trust and governance.

AI already shows strong potential in diagnostics, data analysis, and workflow efficiency. But in health systems, what really matters is how these systems are embedded and governed.

Consistent outputs can create perceived reliability — which, especially in clinical contexts, can quickly lead to overtrust.

That’s why responsible usage is critical:

-clear accountability for decisions
-transparent and explainable outputs
-integration into validated workflows
-continuous human oversight

AI can strengthen health systems — but only if it is used as decision support, not decision authority.

Effective governance is not a barrier to adoption — it is what makes adoption viable at scale.

Welchen Aha-Effekte hatte ich diese Woche...Das eigentliche Problem ist nicht nur der geliehene Schlüssel. Es ist, dass wir das Schloss noch gar nicht eingebaut haben.
Am Beispiel des 29. Juni zeigt das Muster perfekt: finaler Rats-Beschluss zum AI-Omnibus, Start des China-EU-Konsultationsmechanismus.
Zwei Unterschriften, eine Leerstelle - der Text ist fertig, die Kapazität nicht.

𝗘𝗡𝗚: Europe talks a lot about digital sovereignty. But maybe we talk too much about law - and too little about the plug.
Last week I wrote here about the “borrowed key”: Europe’s dependence on China’s rare earths.
This week, it became clear to me that the real problem is not just the borrowed key. It is that we have not even installed the lock.
June 29 captures the pattern perfectly: the Council’s final sign-off on the AI Omnibus, and the launch of the China-EU consultation mechanism. Two signatures, one missing piece - the text is done, the capacity is not.
The AI Omnibus defers its own high-risk deadlines because authorities and standards are not ready.
CADA writes cloud sovereignty into law while European providers sit at roughly 10% market share. And while Europe is still debating sovereignty, US VCs poured $355.9bn into AI in the first half of the year — with two firms alone raising more than ten times the entire InvestAI gigafactory budget.

My take: sovereignty is not what the Official Journal says. It is what reaches the data centre - and what can actually be connected to the grid.

What closes the gap between paper and capacity first: capital, kilowatts or competence? 👇

Digital sovereignty in practice: openDesk as a resilient emergency workplace. 🛡️☁️

Cyberattacks, software outages, or maintenance issues can severely threaten the operational capacity of public administration and critical infrastructure. To tackle this, the CKKI project (Cloud-based Communication for Critical Infrastructures) has successfully demonstrated how open-source collaboration tools can secure communications during crises under real-world conditions.
Together with Zentrum Digitale Souveränität (ZenDiS) and cloud partners IONOS, STACKIT and T-Systems International, the project tested four independent openDesk instances across different cloud platforms.

Key results & insights:

🔹 Real-world Crisis Resilience: Business Continuity Management (BCM) tests confirmed that openDesk modules (email, chat, documents, video) function reliably as a secondary, independent communication channel.
🔹 Multi-Cloud Interoperability: Successfully migrating instances between different cloud providers validated the high flexibility and independence of open-source architectures.
🔹 Concrete Actionability: As ZenDiS CEO Leonhard Kugler highlighted, digital sovereignty is not an abstract concept, but operational readiness when it matters most.

The insights and results from CKKI flow directly into the 8ra Initiative, supporting our mission to build a sovereign, interoperable European cloud-edge infrastructure. By proving that productive software can run seamlessly across multiple cloud providers, CKKI provides a practical blueprint for multi-provider resilience in Europe.

Digital Sovereignty can not be achieved by walling-off or by "Security through Obscurity" - but instead by sharing knowledge, learning from each other, enabling each other and working together towards a fair and open digital ecosystem where everyone can participate on a level playing field.

Open Source is the lever to achieve this mutual goal.

We are thankful for the valuable exchange with the Kenyan Government on questions of digital sovereignty, digital transformation and open-source innovation. We gained many insights and are looking forward to our continued partnership!

[Publicacion compartida de Eng.John Kipchumba Tanui, CBS]
Today, I had the privilege of engaging with the Open Source Business Alliance (OSBA) Delegation from Germany alongside representatives from leading German and European open-source IT companies currently in Nairobi for strategic engagements on digital transformation & open-source innovation.

The delegation, facilitated by GIZ Kenya through the Digital Transformation Center Kenya and the Kenyan-German Digital Dialogue, brought together technology leaders and experts from organizations representing over 270 enterprises across Europe focused on advancing open-source ecosystems and sovereign digital infrastructure.

Among the distinguished officials and industry leaders met were:

• Peter Gietz – CEO, DAASI International
• Martin Pilka – CEO, dNation
• Peer Heinlein – CEO, Heinlein Group & Board Member, OSBA
• Chris Hendriks – CEO, OpenCloud
• Dominik Epple – Senior Solution Architect, Open-Xchange
• Lothar Becker – CEO, Riess Applications / LibreOffice
• Burkhard Noltensmeier – CEO, teuto.net
• Peter Ganten – CEO, Univention
• Joerg Uehlin – Global Digital Jobs Lead, GIZ Kenya
• Amrit Labhuram – Kenyan-German Digital Dialogue Advisor, GIZ Kenya

The discussions focused on strengthening Kenya’s open-source ecosystem through partnerships, policy alignment, local capacity building, and knowledge exchange leveraging European expertise and Kenya’s growing digital economy.

Key areas of engagement included digitizing government services through open-source technologies, supporting procurement reforms, strengthening local technical capacity, and fostering collaboration between Kenyan and European technology ecosystems.

The delegation shared insights from Germany and the European Union on open-source policies and procurement frameworks that prioritize interoperability, digital sovereignty, local value creation, innovation, job creation, and skills development.

The meeting also highlighted opportunities around sovereign cloud infrastructure, secure communication systems, identity and access management, LibreOffice solutions, smart city technologies, data science platforms, and sovereign AI cloud ecosystems.

Kenya expressed strong interest in developing a “Kenya GovStack” — a sovereign stack of open-source solutions — as well as sandbox testing environments, potentially within Konza Technopolis infrastructure, to support validation and deployment of government-ready open-source technologies.

The engagement reaffirmed Kenya’s position as Africa’s Silicon Savannah and a strategic technology hub supported by a highly skilled ICT talent pool, a vibrant innovation ecosystem, and expanding opportunities for regional and global digital partnerships.

The discussions concluded on a strong note of partnership & shared commitment towards advancing Kenya’s digital transformation agenda, strengthening digital sovereignty, and creating sustainable opportunities for Kenyan tech talent and enterprises through deeper collaboration with German and European partners.

Andreas Prins bringt es auf den Punkt. Die Frage ist nicht mehr wann digitale Souveränität real wird, sondern wo sie bereits gelebt wird. CADA gibt diesem Anspruch jetzt einen regulatorischen Rahmen. Wir freuen uns, dass unser Ansatz als konkretes Beispiel wahrgenommen wird!

****

Andreas Prins puts it perfectly. The question is no longer when digital sovereignty becomes real, but where it already is. CADA now gives that standard a regulatory framework. We are glad our approach is being recognized as a concrete example!

[Publicacion compartida de Andreas Prins]
CADA is just released, obviously there are already excellent technology stack that adhere to the highest levels as suggested by CADA. So we no longer need to ask the question: "𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹?" But "𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗱 𝗶𝘁 𝗯𝗲𝗰𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹?"

Earlier today my two colleagues tipped me on what our German partner focusnet has built. They are a Berlin-based managed cloud provider. Fully German owned, data centres in Germany, ISO 27001 certified, GDPR by design. And they just launched a managed SUSE Virtualization offering that, in my view, is one of the most complete practical examples of CADA compliance I have seen.

Here is why that matters.

Six reasons this is a CADA story, not just a product story:
𝟭. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗷𝘂𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗱𝗶𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗶𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝗮𝘁 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝗹𝗮𝘆𝗲𝗿. focusnet is a German GmbH. SUSE is headquartered in Luxembourg with deep European roots. Neither entity falls under US CLOUD Act or equivalent extraterritorial legislation. For CADA assurance levels 3 and 4, that structural immunity is the starting point.
𝟮. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗰𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗔𝗗𝗔 𝘄𝗮𝘀 𝘄𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲𝗻 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁. The Broadcom/VMware acquisition was the real-world demonstration of dependency risk. Prices changed. Licensing changed. European customers had no exit.
𝟯. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗶𝘀 𝗳𝘂𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲. Every component, from the Linux kernel up through Kubernetes and KubeVirt, has publicly accessible source code. An independent assessor can inspect every layer. No NDAs, no proprietary access agreements, no vendor cooperation required. That is what Article 20 of CADA actually asks for.
𝟰. 𝗢𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗱𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲, 𝗼𝗽𝗲𝗻 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲, 𝗯𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗮𝗹. SUSE Virtualization runs on commodity servers. The storage layer is software-defined and open. No proprietary hardware lock-in at any layer. This directly addresses what Article 7(2)(g) requires of national strategies.
𝟱. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗮𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗰𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘃𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗸𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘀 𝗴𝗮𝗽. CADA creates obligations that require expertise most public sector organisations do not have internally. A German MSP running this stack on your behalf gives you the sovereignty outcome without needing internal HCI expertise.
𝟲. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝘅𝗶𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮𝘀 𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝘆. CADA’s interoperability provisions are not satisfied by sovereignty at rest. They require sovereignty in motion — the credible ability to switch without structural penalty. focusnet demonstrated this with their own migration. A customer leaving tomorrow faces no proprietary barrier, no locked data format, no vendor cooperation required.

Most organisations focus on where their data sits. The harder question is what it would actually cost them to leave.

What does your current stack look like against these six criteria? I would love to know where the gaps are.

In Ireland's parliament (Dáil Éireann), Frankie Feighan, Minister for Public Expenditure, Infrastructure, Public Service Reform and Digitalisation, said the recent tender for suppliers to take part in a framework agreement to supply Microsoft software and services had been canceled after "matters of concern were raised by an interested party."

Cian O'Callaghan, deputy leader of the opposition Social Democrats, said "There are a number of alternatives out there that other European countries and states are moving towards. They are doing so for value-for-money reasons, and so they are no longer technologically dependent on the US but can rely on European-regulated services and products. There is LibreOffice, Collabora Online, Open-Xchange, Nextcloud, Thunderbird and openDesk by Germany's Zentrum für Digitale Souveränität der Öffentlichen Verwaltung, ZenDiS, which is a readily assembled government-grade suite."

"The German state of Schleswig-Holstein recently moved 30,000 staff from Microsoft to LibreOffice, Linux, Thunderbird, and Open-Xchange. It is saving more than €15 million a year. The French police, the Gendarmerie Nationale, switched over 100,000 desktops to Linux. They will save roughly €500 million, half a billion, over 15 years."

The continuamce of this debate will be interesting to watch.

Looking back at July, five developments show Europe moving from the ambition of digital sovereignty towards the harder task of making it operational.

📅 7 July - Austrian companies make digital sovereignty a business priority
Seven Austrian companies - including Erste Bank, A1, Anexia, KEBA, SPAR ICS, Umdasch and VIG - launched the Initiative Digitale Souveränität. Its message: sovereignty is not isolation. It means preserving choice, European alternatives and control over critical technologies and data.
Sources: Initiative Digitale Souveränität, APA

📅 7-8 July - Europe connects data sovereignty with cyber resilience
The European Commission presented its Action Plan on Cybersecurity and AI and opened a consultation on European data sovereignty. Together, they address two sides of dependency: who can access European data - and whether Europe can protect the systems through which it flows.
Sources: European Commission, EUR-Lex

📅 9-14 July - The digital euro moves towards implementation
The European Parliament supported negotiations on the digital euro. Five days later, the ECB selected 36 payment providers for a twelve-month pilot, including BAWAG and RBI from Austria. This marked a shift from political commitment to practical testing.
Sources: European Parliament, European Central Bank, Oesterreichische Nationalbank, Reuters

📅 20 July - European banks expose a resilience gap
An AlixPartners survey placed cybersecurity at the top of the risk agenda for European financial-services leaders. Yet fragmented responsibility and constrained resources continue to challenge operational readiness. Sovereignty requires more than infrastructure - it also requires the ability to recover.
Sources: AlixPartners, Börsen-Zeitung

📅 29 July - AI governance becomes a supervisory responsibility
BaFin outlined its role in supervising financial-sector AI under the European framework, including transparency, prohibited practices and high-risk applications such as creditworthiness assessments. Responsible AI is moving from voluntary principles towards evidence, controls and accountability.
Sources: BaFin, Handelsblatt, European Commission

Together, these developments reveal a progression: From ambition to infrastructure. From infrastructure to resilience. From resilience to accountability.

I am proud to be part of #ErsteGroup - one of the European banking groups helping move this conversation from aspiration towards action.
Europe does not need to build everything alone. But it must retain the ability to understand, govern, secure and change the systems on which it depends.
That is the difference between declaring digital sovereignty and making it operational.

For years some people called my architecture old-fashioned. Too many separate systems, too much integration work in the middle. This year the German market started calling the same approach digitale Souveränität, and now it sits on every conference agenda.

The whole conversation here is about getting off the big US hyperscalers. Good goal. But it is becoming a slogan, and the slogan skips the hard part: how do you actually build that independence?

My answer is boring, and it starts by breaking the business into separate parts. Finance lives in SAP. The warehouse runs on its own WMS, transport on a separate TMS, procurement on its own system, sales in a CRM, and even the document flow sits in a dedicated platform. None of them talks straight to another. They all meet in one integration layer in the middle, and that layer belongs to us, not to a vendor.

Because of that, each system is just a component on the bus. A hyperscaler or an AI model is the same - one more component. To replace one, I change a connector. I do not rebuild the business around a new vendor.

And independence is not free. It costs more and moves slower than buying one suite where everything is already wired together. Sometimes the suite is the right call, and I have made that choice too.

So I am still working out the line. Which processes are worth the extra cost to keep independent, and which ones can safely sit inside a vendor you cannot control?

#DigitaleSouveränität #EnterpriseArchitecture #CIO

The primary goals that I have in mind here is (public) procurement, ie. knowing what software is available and who are vendors that I can expect to know about this software. The other would be about managing supply chain risk. But I am sure other use cases could come to mind.

The European Technological Sovereignty Package from European Commission is a major milestone.

The EU Open Source Strategy is a great move in helping to ensure sovereignty, and highlights the need for improved public procurement of open source solutions, better governance frameworks and support for sustainable open source business models to help combat freeriding.

It’s particularly pleasing to see the The Matrix.org Foundation open standard highlighted for vendor-agnostic, sovereign communications.

The European Commission is already using Element’s Matrix-based platform, and Element also powers real time communications for Germany’s BundesMessenger and Zentrum Digitale Souveränität (ZenDiS)'s openDesk, France’s Tchap and LaSuite (from (Direction interministérielle du numérique (DINUM)) and Sweden’s SAFOS Chatt (from Försäkringskassan).

The Matrix open standard ensures governments are not locked into a single vendor. Instead it nurtures an interoperable ecosystem of vendors and providers that drive innovation and healthy competition.

More than 20 European governments already use Matrix to support vendor-agnostic real time communications, replacing the likes of Microsoft Teams, Slack, WhatsApp and Signal.
